utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. Good morning. Mr. President, this is our 57th motion for finding of disclosure violation and for remedial measures. The provision that in this instance was violated was paragraph L of your order on the procedure for the conduct of the trial which provides that the final amalgamated witness statement shall be provided to the Trial Chamber and the accused at least 48 hours prior to the testimony of the witness. There have been three violations of this rule. The first being with the witness Suad Dzafic who testified yesterday on the 1st of September, and his amalgamated statement, final amalgamated statement was not delivered to us until the evening of 31 August. We let that go because we thought perhaps it was an isolated incident. However, last night, we received the final amalgamated statements for the two witnesses who are proposed to testify today, KDZ-606, which was sent by e-mail about 5.35 p.m., which Dr. Karadzic also received after 5 p.m. at the Detention Unit. And which contains comments on 13 documents which had not previously been included in the draft amalgamated statement. The third witness, Sefik Hurko, we received -- it was sent about 8.35 last night. I have to admit I didn't check my e-mail until this morning, but Dr. Karadzic still hasn't received that amalgamated statement, that final amalgamated statement, and it contains new information about new incidents and some additional significant information about incidents that had been previously described by the witness. And so we are asking that you make a finding that there has been a violation on three occasions of the requirements for disclosure, and as a remedy for that, that you postpone the testimony of the next two witnesses until Monday, so Dr. Karadzic can have an adequate time to prepare. We realise that this situation is caused mostly by the pace of the witnesses at this phase of the trial, because we are hearing a lot of short witnesses and we understand it's difficult for the Prosecution, even with all their resources, to keep up with this pace, and, of course, it's extremely difficult for us with about one tenth of those resources. But, in any event, the problem appears to be that the witnesses are not being brought to The Hague in sufficient time to comply with your order, and we think that that problem needs to be addressed and remedied not only for these witnesses but so that the problem doesn't arise in the future. In particular, in our Defence case, we anticipate that the witnesses will need to arrive significantly in advance of their testimony in order to -- for us to properly prepare and disclose the material that will be necessary and so we ask the Chamber to make a finding that there has been violation to postpone the testimony of the two witnesses until Monday, and to make whatever arrangements the Chamber can make to ensure that in the future witnesses are brought to The Hague sufficiently in advance so that the problem doesn't recur. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, I'd like to treat each of the three witnesses that Mr. Robinson has identified in turn. In respect of Suad Dzafic, we did file on the 14th of July, 2011, a draft amalgamated statement as an appendix to the notification in respect of Rule 92 ter for that witness. There is no requirement in Your Honour's order for the conduct of trial that the Prosecution should file a draft amalgamated statement. It's something we do to assist the Defence in their preparation for cross-examination of the witness. The draft amalgamated statement for Mr. Dzafic was practically identical to the final signed version with the addition of some comments on some payment lists which had been admitted in evidence already. Now, in respect of the second witness, that is -- if we can deal with KDZ-606, a draft of the amalgamated statement of that witness was filed on the 25th of August, 2011. The draft amalgamated statement highlighted references to nine additional documents, four of them are simply photographs of sites of mosques in Rogatica, with the specific indication that we intended to show these documents to the witness during proofing. And the rest of the additional information and the final amalgamated statement are corrections of a minor nature made by the witness during proofing yesterday. As Your Honours are aware, the proofing for that witness was slightly postponed due to illness on his part. Let's deal now with the third witness and that is Sefik Hurko. A draft amalgamated statement was filed as an appendix to his 92 ter notification on the 16th of August, 2011. Along with that draft amalgamated statement, we notified the Defence of a number of documents that we might discuss with the witness. Of those documents, we selected three which made their way into the final amalgamated statement. So just to emphasise, the final amalgamated statement simply contains comments on three documents listed in the notification filed on the 16th of August. Other changes in the statement do refer to Rajko Kusic's involvement, for example, in Rasadnik, a scheduled detention facility, Rajko Kusic's role in transferring the witness to a high school in Rogatica, another scheduled detention facility. And Rajko Kusic's role in the cleansing of Rogatica is well heralded in that statement. The witness identifies him as being one of the principal players in Rogatica in 1992. I want to emphasise again that we are doing what we can within the resource constraints of the Tribunal to give the Defence as much advance notification as we reasonably can so that they do have draft amalgamated statements which really cover 90 to 95 per cent of what the witness is going to say, and we are going above and beyond what we are required to do by an order on procedure for conduct of trial. Now, in respect of Mr. Robinson's concern that there have been new comments made by the witness on specific areas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will come to that. Mr. Gaynor, what we ordered in our previous order referred to, that is 8th of October, 2009, order, was that the Prosecution should provide the accused and the Trial Chamber the final amalgamated witness statement at least 48 hours prior to the testimony of the witness. That does not mean that it is always okay to provide that document, statement, two days before. In the same paragraph, we said the amalgamated statement shall be prepared well in advance of the witness arriving in The Hague to testify. Although our order didn't refer to the draft statement, I take it the final witness's amalgamated statement should have been provided at the time when you usually provide with the draft in our past experience. Do you have any observation to that, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President. We -- in many cases, we provide the draft amalgamated statement to the Defence weeks in advance. Now, obviously we haven't yet had a position to confirm that with the witness. The resources don't permit witnesses to be brought to The Hague to review the statement and then to go back to their home, their country of origin, and then to return for testimony. So what we do is we send a draft amalgamated statement which has been prepared well in advance of the witness arriving in The Hague to testify, to the Defence. Now the disclosure of the draft is not required under paragraph L. If Your Honour is asking: Did we comply with the obligation to provide a final amalgamated statement 48 hours before start of testimony, the answer is no, but I'm attempting to put the sequence of events into context to indicate that we have done a considerable amount to facilitate the Defence's preparation of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just before I hear from you, from both of you, I have a question for Mr. Robinson. So the Defence position is that had there not been an addition to the draft statement, you wouldn't have objected to the belated disclosure, if the only change is the witness's signature?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct. I think that we would have considered what we had been provided with earlier to be the final amalgamated statement if it was only the matter of the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So one solution one can think of is that to order the Prosecution to lead the witness live in relation to whatever is contained in the -- added to the previous draft statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think that can be a solution for Witness KDZ-606 because the only differences is his comments on documents that are sought to be admitted as associated exhibits, so if those are led live then I think that we would be in the same position, essentially, as if we have the draft -- there's not many changes to the draft that we received a long time ago. But for the other witness, for Mr. Hurko, there is disclosure of new elements that I think -- first of all, and Dr. Karadzic hasn't seen that statement. That's a Rule 66(A)(ii) statement now because it's not only amalgamating what was earlier disclosed but it contains new elements, and, therefore, we think that we would be prejudiced by the fact that new elements have been added to a statement we just received on the eve of the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's put that aside for the moment because we are not in the position to say anything unless the Chamber is also able to see that document in relation to Rule 66(A)(ii).

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: You should definitely see that document. I think it was maybe copied to Chambers when it was sent to us last night. But if you see there is a track-change version of that statement. And once you see it, you'll see exactly what is at stake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And my last question for Mr. Gaynor is this: Whether it is possible on the part of the Prosecution, instead of trying to incorporate everything witness adds to the existing draft statement, that it leads those evidence live as a kind of change to the previous statement when the witness is in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. I would be willing to do that. Mr. President, can I just point out at this stage that the tracked changes version which I provided to the Defence, there are a couple of paragraphs, four paragraphs, which simply moved position in the statement. Now, due to the way the tracked changes operate, they appear to be new paragraphs. They are simply moved from one part of the statement to the other, but, yes, to answer Your Honour's question, I am willing to lead the new parts live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And has it been your practice that when you provide a final amalgamated statement that has been changed in one way or another from the previous one, you provide a track-change version -- has been practised all the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Not always. In respect of these two witnesses, 606 and Sefik Hurko, we have provided documents showing the new material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I offer the parties to add whatever they want to say in addition to what has been already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think the only thing I would like to emphasise at the end, Mr. President, is that as a trial lawyer, myself, I just absolutely cannot see how Dr. Karadzic could be expected to cross-examine Mr. Hurko without seeing that statement, and I invite you to look at it. And I'll just give you an example: The witness had previously described beatings that he and his father endured, and for the first time in his statement, in this statement we received last night, he acknowledges that he was found to be in possession of a number of bullets and a -- his father had a pistol and that was the reason they were beaten. That's just one example. Another example is a description of sexual misconduct at one of the facilities. He's given -- recounted a completely new incident that had not been disclosed, that we were not aware of before. So those are two examples of the new material that's contained in that. So I know that you want to move forward and not delay the trial, but in this particular instance, besides the violation of the Rule itself, there is prejudice because of Dr. Karadzic's not having seen that material. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just add one word from the point of view of drafts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can read one statement, only once. That's my rhythm. If I get a draft and if I study the draft, and then if I get the final version of the amalgamated statement, that is two readings and I don't have time for that. Hence, the draft would not really help me much. I need 48 hours to get the final version. Technically speaking, that's the way it is. Mr. Robinson simply doesn't know that because I've never told him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have a similar experience on my part because we give it a read before -- well in advance of the draft whether those alleged associated exhibits are part -- are forming indispensable and inseparable parts of the witness statement. And then I find very many -- recently new passages added in the final amalgamated statement in relation to those exhibits. So I had to compare, just once again, just the day before the witness's evidence. That's why I asked whether there is -- a track-change versions have been offered in the previous time. Unless you have anything to add, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. I'd simply want to make the point when we balance the advantages and disadvantages, that in our submission, it is, in fact, advantageous for the Defence to have in writing, prior to the witness's testimony, new evidence which he wishes to give, as opposed to a situation where the witness might be called live by the Prosecution and the new material arrives literally in the courtroom while we are all listening to that material. So that is one factor to take into account when we add material to a statement which is then disclosed to the Defence. That was my only additional observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just mention that we would still expect that material to be disclosed through a proofing note even if it's not in the amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will rise for 15 minutes to consider this matter. --- Break taken at 9.22 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having reviewed the submission of the parties, and giving -- having given careful consideration to the matter, the Chamber's conclusions are as follows: In relation to KDZ-606, we order the Prosecution to lead the witness live in relation to the information which has been added to the previous draft amalgamated statement. Given that the added information is not that significant, and also having considered the submission of Mr. Robinson on this matter, the Chamber is of the view that the Defence is able to cross-examine the witness today. In relation to Mr. Hurko, while the Chamber will order the Prosecution lead the witness live in relation to the added information, as in the case of KDZ-606, the Chamber postpones the cross-examination of this witness to Monday, given the size and scope of added information, as well as the alleged 66(A)(ii) violation which will be considered by the Chamber separately. For the future conduct of the trial, the Chamber very much encourages the Prosecution to continue its practice of offering draft amalgamated statements. However, the Chamber encourages the Prosecution to comply with its 48-hours deadline in offering their final version of amalgamated statement, as well as offering a track-change versions when there is any changes from previously disclosed draft statements. Mr. Gaynor, who will be the next witness we hear first?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Hurko is here, and he's ready to go, and KDZ-606 is being brought to the Tribunal as we speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then what we are going to do is to hear the examination-in-chief of Mr. Hurko and we will postpone the cross-examination of the witness to Monday, and then we proceed to hear evidence of KDZ-606.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President, can I just ask for one item of clarification. It wasn't my understanding that the Defence had asserted a Rule 66(A)(ii) violation. It was a violation of Your Honour's order on the procedure for the conduct of trial. I'd invite Mr. Robinson, perhaps, to clarify his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What I understand -- yes, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly correct and I was going to rise for that very same reason. Because the material was not in the Prosecution's possession until yesterday, this new information, then its disclosure didn't violate Rule 66(A)(ii), but the nature of the material was such that it obligated them to disclose it, but they didn't disclose it late, they disclosed it on time. But we do ask the Chamber to make a specific finding that paragraph L of your order has been violated on each of the three occasions in which we alleged so that that's part of the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. There is no dispute that there's a non-compliance with that order in relation to these two witnesses. Yes, let's call your next witness, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The next witness is Sefik Hurko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could kindly take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Good morning, Mr. Hurko, do you follow the proceedings in the language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: For the record, could you state your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Sefik Hurko, that's my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You're from the municipality of Rogatica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes, the municipality of Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What is the name of the village from which you come?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Village is Madzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you know the location of Kopljevici?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Where is Madzer in relation to Kopljevici?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Madzer is before Rogatica. It is six kilometres away from Rogatica, whereas the other village is about a kilometre and a half away in the other direction, towards Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In a statement which you gave in 1994, you said that you stayed in the neighbourhood of Rudo with your father, your mother and your family from the 6th of April 1992. Where is Rudo?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Rudo is in Rogatica. That's a neighbourhood in Rogatica. That's where I lived with my wife and children. That's where we had sublet an apartment. When the war started, I went to the village of Madzer where I was born. That's where my father, mother and grandmother lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Take you now to the 22nd May, 1992. On that date, you were in Madzer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: The 22nd of May, I was in the village of Madzer where my father lived. On that day, around 1300 hours, fire was opened at all Muslim villages in the municipality of Rogatica; that is to say, literally all of them. And that is when that happened for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How do you know that fire was opened on all the Muslim villages in the municipality of Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: The village of Madzer is up a hill, and you can see all of Rogatica and the other villages like Kovalj, Vragolovi, Kopljevici, Orahovo, Sljedovici, Cubrici. All of these villages could be seen and you could see the shells falling on all of these villages. You could see all of that from this village of mine where I was, Madzer, and also these shells were falling on Madzer, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to call up now, please, 07859.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, the screen in front of you, on the left, do you see a document which appears to have been issued by Rajko Kusic, addressed to the Supreme Command of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and to Sokolac TO commander?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes, I see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In the first sentence, do you see that on the 22nd of the 5th, 1992, the author states: "We conducted armed operations with military police company against enemy strongholds in the villages of Dub, Pokrivenik, Kopljevici," and he names other places, including Rudo 2 settlement?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: I see that. Dub, Pokrivenik, Kopljevici, I know all of that. Rudo, as I told you, is a neighbourhood in Rogatica. That's the day when the war started. So in this area, from Madzer to Visegrad, the population was predominantly Muslim, so these were Muslim villages; that is to say that the population was 90 per cent Muslim. There were no strongholds there then. All these people were civilians who had left Rogatica earlier on. I think that the fighting was over by then in Visegrad. Visegrad had been liberated and there were refugees in the area. In Gorazde, there was fighting, and there was about 35 square kilometres there and there were refugees all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I just want to confirm: Were you aware of any enemy strongholds in any of the villages named in that document?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: I've just said that there were no strongholds whatsoever, of all these people there were civilians, in all of these places.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3265, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to call up now, please, 65 ter 08538.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The document on the screen in front of you appears to bear at the bottom the date 23rd of the 5th, 1992, and commander Rajko Kusic is the name which appears at the bottom of this document. As you can see, Mr. Hurko, Mr. Kusic in this document appears to be ordering units to hold their positions towards Kusturice, Oskoplje, and Rakitnica. And he orders that in the following 24 hours, the operations unit shall mop up Oskoplje, Kusturice, Zakome and Kalimanici with the assistance of Sokolac. Could you tell us the ethnic makeup, as far as you're aware, of the four settlements of Oskoplje, Kusturice, Zakome and Kalimanici.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Kusturice is Muslim; Oskoplje, Muslim; Rakitnica, Muslim; and Cadove, Muslim. Muslims lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Are you aware of the presence of any armed Muslim formations in those locations on the 22nd of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: This is opposite the place where I was staying, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you observe any troops commanded by Rajko Kusic, who you believe to be commanded by Rajko Kusic, in action?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: The 14th of August, when I was taken prisoner, that's when I found out that Rajko Kusic was commander of the Serb army in Rogatica. That's when I saw him and that is how he introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We will come to that date in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In the meantime, I'd like to tender that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think the witness has really confirmed anything about that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I believe the witness has given us information about the ethnic makeup of the four settlements where Kusic is ordering the operations unit to carry out mop-up operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's all that he gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, the Chamber will not admit this document through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like to move ahead to the 14th of August. You have previously in your statement of the 16th of November, 1994, described your arrest by four Serb soldiers, and you said that they took you to a garage by the house of a person called Andric. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What was the first name of the Andric?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mico Andric, the house of Mico Andric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I just had a question about whether this witness was being led viva voce or whether there was going to be any use made of the amalgamated statement. So I -- as I'm hearing it, I'm thinking this is a viva voce witness, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My understanding is that Mr. Gaynor is going to lead live in relation to the information that has been added, and then he will proceed to tender the 92 ter statement. Am I understanding correct, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Absolutely correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you were taken to the garage by the house of Mico Andric. And in your previous statement you said that you were beaten up there. Who beat you there?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: I was arrested, my mother, my father and my cousin, Hurko Abdulah, were arrested in the village of Madzer. I said we were brought in in the garage of Mico Andric in the village of Kosovo. It's about four kilometres away from the village of Madzer. We were brought there. We were sitting in front of the house for 20 or 30 minutes. Soldiers began to arrive. When the soldiers arrived, four soldiers told us to enter the garage. When we entered the garage, the soldier -- there was a soldier with a mustache. He was shorter than I was, perhaps 1.75 metres tall, and he asked us if we knew a certain person. I said we didn't know him. He said, I'm Rajko Kusic, the commander of the Serbian army in Rogatica. Stojan Perkovic was with him. Also Brane Krsmanovic, aka Pipa, and Danko Neric. There was a bench there. We sat there next to each other. My father first, then me, then my mother, and then my cousin. Then Rajko Kusic said to Brano Krsmanovic and to Perkovic to search us. Stojan Perkovic found in my pocket 70 bullets from a 7.62-millimetre pistol for which I did have a licence from before the war. He took the ammunition and hit me on the head, and this ammunition just spilled all over this garage. Krsmanovic, Brane approached my father and began to tell him to stick his tongue out, he took a knife out to cut his tongue off. He started to cut his ears and then he took my ammunition and made me eat three or four of those bullets in the garage. And I did eat them. Then they continued to beat us. My father fell to the ground. He was already all covered in blood. Stojan Perkovic then took out a knife and then he started to stab me in my hands, then he wanted to slash my throat. I put my hands up there so I was all covered with blood as well. I don't know how long that lasted. Kusic brought me outside, then -- and then Danko Neric was there, too. He was holding a rifle and Kusic only had a pistol. He said that I should start to talk about something. He said I -- he wasn't interested, I should start talking about something else. I mean, it wasn't any good what I was talking about, and he wasn't interested in what I was saying either. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If I can interrupt for a moment. Was Rajko Kusic present when you were forced to eat the bullets?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Rajko Kusic was present the whole time, when I was eating the bullets and while everything else was going on. He was there the whole time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just briefly say something about the transcript so that all of these mistakes don't pile up? The witness said he was captured, and the transcript says once "taken prisoner," and the second time "arrested." And this is something that I've been pointing to the whole time that semantically these are quite different things, so I would kindly ask the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber will bear that in mind in reading the transcript. And there will be another opportunity to correct the transcript, if necessary. In any event, thank you for your intervention. We will proceed. Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I want to clarity another point which you've eluded to: Was Rajko Kusic present when you and your father were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Were you then taken -- I believe in your previous statement you said you were taken by car, that is, you, your father, and your mother, to the secondary school centre in Rogatica and imprisoned there. My question is this: Who was in the car, taking you from Andric's garage to Rogatica secondary school centre?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: I just want to say first that in the garage, where we were beaten, at one point Dragomir Abazovic came and Rajko asked him what is he going to do with us, and he said that the three of us, me, my father and my mother, should be taken to Rogatica and to interrogate my cousin. And then when we stood up, this Stojan Perkovic and Brane Krsmanovic immediately started to beat him. They put his hands in his mouth, they began to hit him, use the knifes, that they had. He started moaning and screaming, and they took him outside and killed him. I am asserting that they killed him because he never appeared again. Then, when they came out, there was a vehicle, a caddy vehicle with only two seats in the front. They put my mother, my father and me in the back. The driver was Danko Neric. Next to him, Rajko Kusic sat, and they took us to the high school centre in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What was the name of the person you describe as your cousin who was killed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Abdulah Hurko.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like to request document 65 ter 07336, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The events you've been describing took place on the 14th of August, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The document which is appearing on the screen in front of you is dated 15th of the 8th, 1992, addressed to the General Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and to the command of the SRK. At the bottom, it appears to have been issued by commander Rajko Kusic. Now, you see in this document that Kusic refers to enemy forces, yesterday, that being the 14th of August, 1992, in the villages of Orahovo and Kopljevici. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Where exactly were you arrested on the 14th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: In the village of Madzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Where is that in relation to Kopljevici?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: It's before Kopljevici in the direction of Rogatica, some one to two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Were -- the forces who arrested you, who were they commanded by?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Rajko. You mean when I was arrested, at that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: There were three soldiers there, three Serbian soldiers from Rogatica. I knew them, just by sight. Milica Pecanica [phoen] I knew well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Who did you believe to be the commander of those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Rajko Kusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This document refers to operations by members of the Rogatica Brigade in the villages of Kopljevice and Orahovo. Is that consistent with what you observed on that day?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3266, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like to move to the 15th of August, 1992. In your statement, you say that Danko Neric and a person called Krsman came to pick you up in a car. Would you like to correct the name Krsman?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Brane Krsmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: They were picking you up from what location?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: From the secondary school centre in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You state that they took you towards the village of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: They left you and your father with a soldier at crossroads in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes. Well, perhaps I can talk about what happened that -- a little bit from Rogatica on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like you to describe the incident where a bus arrived. That's the incident I'd like you to describe. If you can describe that briefly, when the bus arrived at the crossroads in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: My father and I came in this Golf vehicle to the village of Kosovo at the crossroads towards Duljevac. Danko Neric was driving, Brane Krsmanovic was sitting next to him, and there was a FAP 13 truck that was following us. The FAP was driven by Sinan Catic. And then at the crossroads there was a soldier, and we were told to get out there, my father and I. And this Brane Krsmanovic said: These two should stay here. And when the bus comes, they should get on the bus. They drove off in the car, and this FAP truck continued towards Duljevac. Then in about 15 or 20 minutes, I'm not sure exactly how long, this minibus came and there was a board on it, "Rogatica-Istanbul," it was a Centrotrans Rogatica bus. It stopped. It was driven by Radisav Rubinac, called Pjano. When the bus stopped, the car was coming back then from the direction of Duljevac, and they said there that my father and I should not get on the bus because Rajko Kusic had to interrogate us about something. Then the car went back, followed by the bus, and they left. After a while, this can be 15 minutes, 20 minutes, half an hour, I cannot remember, I was all bloodied because the day before I had been beaten, then firing started, shooting, from the direction of Duljevac, and when the shooting stopped, when Krsmanovic, Brane came back, and this Danko Neric and this soldier who was there, Brane Krsmanovic told me, We have killed all the balijas. Danko Neric took my father to Rajko Kusic to some place in some house and they took me back to Mico Andric's house, where I was arrested and brought the day before. This was on the 15th of August. It was the second day of my captivity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you in your statement describe your transfer to the detention facility at Rasadnik. Is it correct that that took place the next morning, as you say, which is the 16th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes. On the 16th of July, I was in the secondary school centre, and a truck came with a tarpaulin with policemen. They came and said everyone should get on to the truck and they were going to the Rasadnik camp. Only they mentioned some families who should -- who were loyal who should return.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked to repeat the names of the families.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then in two hours --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I interrupt to seek your clarification on two point. First of all, you said: "On the 16th of July, I was in the secondary school centre." Did you, in fact, mean the 16th of August?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, August, August. August, yes. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Second, you said the names of certain families who the interpreters did not catch. Could you repeat their names, please?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: The families were Hodzic, Soso [phoen], Pasic, and another family were told because -- because they were loyal, they were told that they could go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, was -- is it the case that a person called Kojic gave the order that all the loyal Muslims should be released?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes. The person who came, that was Kojic, he was the one who said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And in your previous statement, you described him as being from the Serbian MUP. In the interests of clarification, did you mean the MUP from Serbia, or did you mean the --

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: No, no, not from Serbia. But since Rogatica was seized and Serbs were there, what I was thinking of was Rogatica, from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When you arrived in Rasadnik, you've described in your previous statement a conversation you had with Mujo Jasarevic about the prisoners who had been taken away to collect hay. Do you recall that conversation?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: I do. In two hours a car came again. They took me and my mother to the secondary school centre, to the same prison. They put me in a cell which is where I saw a number of prisoners. One of them was Mujo Jasarevic. There was some bags, travelling bags, standing there in a corner. There were about 15 bags and some cans of peas, and I said What are these bags? They said that there were about 30 more prisoners, that they had gone to Duljevac to collect the hay, and the tins allegedly was where people -- that people used to relieve themselves because nobody was allowed to leave the prison or the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the prisoners who were taken away to collect hay?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: In some 20 to 30 days, Radisav, Pjano, this person that they called Pjano who was the bus driver told Mujo in front of me, he said, They killed your father over there in Jivistit [phoen] I saved you, you were also supposed to be killed. And then Mujo and I had found out that those people were killed over there. I don't know if anybody survived or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I now propose to go into private session briefly for the next portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In your previous statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In your previous statement, you have described instances of sexual assault of detainees at Rasadnik. Yesterday, you described to me one incident in particular that you wanted to testify about.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: In early December, the prison commander was Vinko Bojic, who came there. He was appointed by Rajko Kusic to the post. At that time, in December, he killed two Muslims who were in the camp. One was Ibro Karaman, the other one was Himzo Brankovic. And in late December, until the 21st of March, there was a lot of sexual mistreatment. They would be taking away men and women to this room where Vinko Bojic was, as the commander of the camp, and then there were three other rooms leading from that room where Serbs were serving their sentences, and there was a Muslim soldier in also one of those rooms. One evening Mujo Jasarevic, Semso Vatres and myself, Dzemo Jamakovic and another person was summoned by Brane Paunic to enter Vinko's office. When we came to the office, we saw four or five Serbian soldiers there who had beards. They had some sort of insignia on their caps, black caps with some insignia on them, skull and cross bones, something like that. They had ammunition belts, you know, the belts with the ammunition. There were rifles there, and they were sitting at Vinko's desk. And I could see four women, Muslim women, who were in the camp. I know their names but I don't want to mention them now. If necessary, I will. He said when we entered that we should strip. We started begging, Why should we strip? He took some bat and said, Come on, take your clothes off. He started shouting so we all started to take our clothes off. The women had already started to take their clothes off, and then we were all naked. And then when we took all of our clothes off, he said we should hold each other's hands and dance, to dance the kolo [phoen] dance, and then we were dancing around those Serb soldiers, Chetniks. I don't even know how to call them. I don't know what sort of soldiers they were. They were people who were there. This took an hour, hour and a half. They made us touch their breasts and made them touch us, but I don't really want to describe that. And then there were three rooms leading off from that office, and then they made a woman enter one of those rooms, naked. She stayed up there for some 20 minutes and then she came out by herself. When she came out of the room, they would -- made another one go in and this lasted for an hour or two. Then they commanded that we should get ready, that they would take us to the room. This was one occasion. And it happened to me on three or four occasions, as well. And it wasn't the same people each time. It was different men, different women each time. And that is the most difficult time for me. When I was eating bullets, when I was beaten, none of that is as bad as the trauma that I carry for the rest of my life because of that. Even when I think of those women, I mean even now when I meet any of them, I just hide. This is something that Vinko Bojic ordered.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we in semi-private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest that we get the names under seal, the names of the persons who were mistreated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll leave it in Your Honour's discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Mr. Hurko, in the course of your answer, you said that you can give the names of those women. We are in private session, which means that nobody else outside, other than us, can hear the proceedings, nor can they read the transcript of our proceedings. Now you had the -- heard the request from Mr. Karadzic. Are you minded to give the names of those women or the ladies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If you can provide the names, please, Mr. Hurko.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: (redacted) These are four women who were there. That was on that particular occasion that I described on that day. But there were other women who had been taken there the following days. I don't know what they did to them then. I'm just talking about the things that I saw myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hurko.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I suggest the witness said that he was abused like this three or four times. Was it always the same women, and if not, can we have the names of those other women as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you can explore that in your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We can return to open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd now like to turn to the question of Rajko Kusic at Rasadnik. This is on paragraph 44 for the other participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you ever see Rajko Kusic at Rasadnik while you were there?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: About six or seven times he came to the prison there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What years did you -- were those six or seven times?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: It was in 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you form any impression as to whether he had any control whatsoever over Rasadnik?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it permissible to ask for impressions?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm going to get to the facts which led to that impression in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Hurko, did you form an impression as to whether Rajko Kusic exercised any control over Rasadnik?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: To what extent did you believe he was in control of that detention place?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Fully, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, could you describe any particular incident which led you to believe that?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Around the 23rd of July, 1993, he entered the room that we were in. He said: I'm not going to feed you any more here. I've been feeding you until now. I'm going to have you transferred to Alija. You're going to be exchanged. I don't need you any more. That was around the 23rd. Not necessarily that particular day, but around the 23rd of July, 1993. During the next two or three days, a bus came, one or two buses came, and they said that we would be exchanged in Bijeljina and that that's where we were going. We all boarded these buses around the 25th, and we arrived in Vlasenica. They only negotiated, talked about something. They didn't reach any agreement. Then we arrived in Zvornik. I don't know what the name of that room is where we were in Zvornik, and they said, You're going to spend the night here, and you're going to continue your journey to Bijeljina on the next day, Batkovic, where the prison was there. We entered that room. It was empty, totally empty. We lay on some parquet floor, and in the morning, around 5.00, a soldier came. He introduced himself as the commander of the Serb army in Zvornik. He started cursing. He was saying all sorts of things, using swear words about our mothers, what are you doing there, lying there? You're going to be exchanged. He said, Get out. And we did get out. There was a truck there covered with a tarpaulin. And we all entered that truck. There were old women there that we had to carry, and so on, but anyway, we were like sardines, packed in that truck. We set off to Bijeljina, Batkovic. We arrived in the Batkovic prison. When we arrived there, they said that we should all get off that truck and a soldier said to us, Now, when I call out your names, women are going to go on to one side and men to the other side. And he started calling out people's names. And once he was halfway done, roughly, another Serb soldier came to him and then they talked for about five minutes. After, that this soldier said, All of you get into that truck again. So we all got into that truck. And the truck left, and returned us to Rogatica, to the prison where we had been before. We arrived in Rogatica around 5.00 or 6.00 in the early evening, that is to say, about 1700 or 1800 hours. Around 2100 hours or 2200 hours, Rajko Kusic and Vinko Bojic arrived. They entered the room, and you could see that this Rajko was nervous. We always had to jump up, and when we got up, and he said, Get up and sit down, and he said that several times. And then he started cursing, and he said, You see, Alija doesn't want you there. No one wants you. I don't know what to do with you. I'm going to call the International Red Cross to take you wherever. I don't need you any more. He also said that we should stand there and then he left. About ten minutes later, Vinko Bojic returned and said that we should sit down. Then on the 28th -- so that was around the 25th. And then on the 28th, the International Red Cross came to register us. Can I go on about that now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, you can. And I'd like you just to explain very briefly, if you can, what it was you said to the Red Cross representatives and what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: The International Red Cross came on the 28th of July 1993. I have that paper that I got then. Rajko Kusic was in Vinko's office when this jeep came, or whatever the name of the vehicle was; it said International Red Cross. And they entered this office of Vinko Bojic. They talked about something there and about ten minutes later, these people from the International Red Cross entered our cell as well as Vinko Bojic. We got up and they said that we should sit down. We did sit down. We introduced ourselves -- or, rather, they introduced themselves and said, We are from the International Red Cross. Don't worry, no people from the Serb military can be here. They told Vinko to leave, and they said, You are free to tell us everything, what you're doing here and how things are here. I was glad. I thought that I had survived and that I would never be beaten again. And I got up and I said that we were being taken to the front line, that we could not survive, that we did not have enough food. That it was hard for us, that they were beating us, that they were taking us every night, that they were mistreating us sexually, that they were stripping us naked, and so on. And also Mujo Jasarevic said a few things, and my father said that he would like it if we could be transferred to another country altogether. They said that they would give Mujo and me some cards stating that we were registered with this International Red Cross because we talked. As for the others, they said that they would be back in two weeks' time and that they would register all of them as well. Is that the words you use, "register"? What's -- what is the word? Well, anyway, yes. Well, they registered us with the International Red Cross, yes. They said that they would bring us some clothes in about 15 days and then they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I would now like to -- you to tell us about an incident which happened around three days later. Keep your comments fairly brief on this.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: About a three days later, after the Red Cross left, Hasim Dumanovic and Nazif Dumanovic were called in. They were there for about half an hour. And after that, Brano Planojevic came and said, Sefik Hurko should go to Vinko's. When I walked in, I saw that those two had been beaten up badly, these were old men, they were 65 years old. As for the place where Vinko was sitting in that office, Dragomir Abazovic, nicknamed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpreter] Was sitting there. I already mentioned him in connection with the situation when I was being taken prisoner. Vinko was there with a baton in his hand and this Abazovic said to me, Sele - I mean, he knew me very well, and he was born in 1957 - as for that statement, when we arrested you, in Kosovo, the statement you gave, it does not tally at all. We captured another Muslim, and now you're going to tell us how things were. I had barely started talking when Vinko started hitting me in the head with his hands. He started hitting me, and also he cocked his pistol, put it in my mouth, and I could not say anything. After that, he said Take off your shirt. I took off my shirt. Then he started plucking hairs from my underarm and made me eat it. And then he started extinguishing cigarettes on my arms. And after that, he told me to strip naked. I was wearing underwear and a jacket and I had to strip. And then they started taunting me quite a bit. And then he took a knife, and then he wanted to hit me in the ribs. And that is when I moved a bit and then he said, Fuck you. What are you doing? You're defending yourself. And he didn't hit me with the tip of the knife, but he turned it around and he used that other part to hit me in the ribs and that's when I fell. There was no air in my lungs any more, it was about five minutes or so, and they kept saying, shouting, Get up, get up. And then I finally managed to get up and I only managed to put my underwear on. A few minutes later, they said that Fejzo Hurko should be called in. That's my father. When they called him in, Vinko started hitting him on the head with both hands. He hit him several times in the head and then he kept saying, Do you want to be taken out? Do you want to be taken to Germany, abroad? All the things that I said to the International Red Cross -- and that I had said to the International Red Cross, that is what they were repeating as they were beating us. Then he started hitting him with the truncheon, too, and then he told him to face the wall and he gave me the truncheon and said that I should beat him. I took the truncheon in my left hand because I did not have enough air in my lungs to use my right-hand. And then I hit him about four or five times. I couldn't do anymore. And then he said, If you cannot do it then I'm going to do it, and then he took that truncheon, I remember that full well. He hit him very strongly 15 times and he did not fall. After the 15th blow, he fell on the floor. He started screaming, moaning. And at that moment, Abazovic, Dragomir and Vinko Bojic left the room. Vinko Bojic had a car, a luxury car, a Stojadin. They got into that car and they left. And they said to Brano Planojevic to take us to the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for the record, could you confirm the nickname of Dragomir Abazovic, which the interpreters just didn't catch a little earlier.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Pidje is his nickname, Dragomir Abazovic's nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll just clarify one or two minor details. You said in your statement then on the 18th of December, 1993, Sejfo Mirvic, a prisoner from the solitary cell, was killed. And then you said in the original statement that somebody came in respect of his death. Who was it that came and what did they do?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please start his answer again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hurko, if you could kindly start your answer from the beginning, they couldn't catch your first part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Satorovic is the name. Tmurni Do. These are places where most of the Muslims stayed on as loyal citizens. They were expelled, too, but at that time they still called them loyal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Hurko, can I just ask you this: After Sejfo Mirvic was killed, is it correct that a doctor came to confirm his death?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, you state that you were transferred from Rasadnik to Kula prison on the 30th of April, 1994, and you describe work that you were required to carry out at Ekonomija. Describe briefly what Ekonomija is and where it is.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Ekonomija is close to Kula. The Serbs called it Ekonomija. That was a farm. Grass was cut, potatoes were dug. I don't know how to explain this. Agricultural activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in a statement which you gave to representatives of the Tribunal in 1999, you gave a list of people who you believed were members of the Crisis Staff for the municipality of Rogatica. One of those you named was Milovan Lelek. Do you wish to make any correction as to whether you believe he was a member of the Rogatica Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: I do, by all means. Milovan Lelek. I don't want that name to be mentioned at all here. I saw this man in civilian clothes. He was very fair, very correct. He always greeted me. When I saw him in civilian clothing, there was something wrong with his knee. He was being treated for that. And I don't know how come that man's name is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You don't believe he was a member of the Rogatica Crisis Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: I just saw him in Rogatica once in civilian clothes. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, what I propose to do is to ask the Rule 92 ter questions in respect to the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Witness, did you have the opportunity to review, with me and with an interpreter, yesterday, a statement to which you made some corrections and clarifications?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I call up, please, 65 ter 90269?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you see on the screen in front of you the first page of that statement?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you adopt that statement as your evidence, and if you were asked questions on the same subjects today, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Well, what I see here is my first and last name and when I was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Hurko, you had an opportunity to review your 1994 statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You then made some corrections and clarifications and additions to that statement. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yesterday it was explained to you that this represents an English translation of your previous statements incorporating the clarifications and additional information which you provided; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You then signed the first and last pages of the statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he put initials on each page. Why don't we show him every page, just go through the document. You'll see the entire document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The last page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, the witness's signature is actually on the penultimate page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. Hurko, do you adopt that statement as your evidence, and if you were asked questions on the same subjects today would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now I'd like to tender that statement in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3267, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I do have a summary of the statement for the public which I can read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Hurko is a Bosnian Muslim from Rogatica. He describes the attack on his village on the 22nd of May, 1992. Mr. Hurko then joins the BiH Territorial Defence. On or around 14th of August, 1992, Serb forces arrested Mr. Hurko, his parents and his uncle at his parents' house. They were taken to a garage by the house of Mico Andric. There, in the presence of Rajko Kusic, Serb soldiers brutally beat Mr. Hurko and his father, and forced Mr. Hurko to swallow bullets. Kusic questioned Mr. Hurko and personally escorted Mr. Hurko and his parents to Rogatica where they were detained in the Veljko Vlahovic secondary school. Kusic took Mr. Hurko's father for further interrogation at the Rogatica police station. On the 15th of August, 1992, Mr. Hurko saw a group of men being transported on a minibus and later heard the sounds of gunfire from the direction in which the bus had travelled. He later became aware that this gunfire may have related to detainees who had been taken from a detention facility at Rasadnik and then killed. Mr. Hurko and his father were transferred to the Rasadnik facility where Mr. Hurko was detained for over 20 months. He saw Rajko Kusic several times there in 1992 and 1993, and formed the view that Kusic had complete control over the prison. Rasadnik was guarded by Serb military police. The warden, Vinko Bojic, was appointed by Rajko Kusic. Bojic subjected both male and female detainees to acts of grossly humiliating mistreatment. Several detainees who were sent to Bojic's office were beaten to death there or shot dead. Mr. Hurko was forced to carry out labour assignments while he was a detainee at Rasadnik, including recovering the bodies of dead soldiers, Serb soldiers, in mined areas. At one stage, Mr. Hurko and other detainees were transferred from Rasadnik to Batkovic camp where they were led to believe they were to be exchanged but were then returned to Rasadnik. On 30th of April, 1994, a group of detainees, including women and children, were transferred from Rasadnik to KP Dom Kula. Mr. Hurko was finally exchanged on the 5th of October, 1994. Now, unless there are other matters, that ends the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gaynor. Mr. Hurko, due to some procedural matters, and also given that there is another witness who is not well, the Chamber wants to conclude his evidence during the course of today. We have to postpone your cross-examination to Monday. So please accept my apologies for your inconvenience but I hope you do understand the situation of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, we'll have a break. Shall we have a break now? We will have a break about half an hour. And we resume at 25 past with the next witness, whose evidence I believe will be heard in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Edgerton. Although the blinds are down, we started in open session because there is one matter I want to clarify in relation to the previous witness. So I have to discuss it with you, Mr. Tieger, because you were there. It may be prudent if we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 5th day of September, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.
